question: What is Netflix's theatrical window policy as of the 3Q26 call?
expected: Traditional 45-day window for a handful of films (e.g. Narnia), not all films as Sally Barton's note says.

result.answer:
Netflix does not have a single, uniform theatrical window. On the 3Q26 call, Ted Sarandos said Netflix is "a streaming first business" and that each film gets its own "bespoke release pattern" [1]. He described a split approach:
- Specialty releases: a 47-day platform theatrical window, e.g., La Bola Negra (the transcript renders the title inconsistently) [2].
- Big family films: an announced 45-day window with a wide theatrical release, for Greta Gerwig's Narnia: The Magician's Nephew and the animated Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory [2].
- IMAX: for the David Fincher film The Adventures of Cliff Booth, Netflix did a deal with IMAX to put it on the biggest screens for a couple of weeks, 4 weeks before the Netflix release [2].
- Sarandos summarized that the strategy now includes "a traditional 45-day window for a handful of films." Netflix is also now reporting box office grosses for these releases [3].
- Volume: about 30 films released theatrically this year, roughly the same as last year [1].

Note error: Sally Barton's 3Q26 note says Netflix is "moving to a standard 45-day theatrical window for all of its films" [4]. The transcript does not support that. Sarandos described a 45-day window for a handful of films, a 47-day window for specialty releases, and a 4-week IMAX-first deal for Cliff Booth [2][3].

citations.passage: And yes, we're going to release about 30 films theatrically this year, pretty much what we did last year. And each 1 of these have their own kind of bespoke release pattern.
So for specialty releases, we're doing a 47-day window platform theatrical release for La Boulange right now.

It's involved to include a traditional 45-day window for a handful of films -- but the other 1 that's been important to folks is that we are also now reporting box office grosses for those releases when we do it.

citations.document: Netflix Earnings Results Notes - 3Q26 - Sally Barton.pdf
citations.passage: Separately, Netflix is moving to a standard 45-day theatrical window for all of its films, a notable shift for a streaming-first company, and is now reporting box office.

question: What GSIB surcharge did JPMorgan say it needs to plan for, and by when?

result.answer:
On the 1Q26 call, CFO Jeremy Barnum said JPMorgan needs to plan for a GSIB surcharge of 5.2% in 2028. That is a 70 basis point increase from the current 4.5% requirement [1]. Combined with the RWA increase from the Basel III Endgame NPR, he said this means a total increase of about $20 billion of GSIB capital on the current balance sheet [1]. He also said the surcharges for almost all GSIBs are scheduled to rise meaningfully over the next two years because of recent growth in the system [2].

it's important to understand that under the current rule, the surcharges for almost all of the GSIB banks are scheduled to increase meaningfully over the next two years simply as a result of recent growth in the system despite, in our view, no change in real-world systemic risk.

question: What Azure growth did Microsoft guide to for FY27 Q2, and what did it say the guide depends on?

result.answer:
On the FY27 Q1 call (Oct 28, 2026), CFO Amy Hood guided FY27 Q2 (Oct–Dec 2026) Azure revenue growth of 49–50% in constant currency. That compares with 48% reported in Q1. She tied it to continued CPU and GPU efficiency gains that help offset some third-party (3P) GPU-as-a-service contracts delayed to H2. She also said customer demand continues to exceed available supply [1][2].

What the guide depends on (from the Q&A):

- Offsetting delayed supply. Some supply Microsoft was counting on in Q2 moved out to H2, so the efficiency work has to help cover that [3].
- Token pricing. Hood said there is "some unknown on some token pricing through the quarter." Q1 token pricing came in higher than expected, and "That stuff can change" [3][4].
- She felt good about guiding on the efficiency gains she could see, but said other things "are less predictable" [3].

Beyond Q2, she said growth will reflect the timing and scale of engineering efficiencies, new capacity adds, and a strong prior-year comparable [1].

Analyst notes match this. Sally Barton's note says the guide depends on more efficiency gains and uncertain token pricing. Joe Smith's and Barton's notes both cite the 49–50% figure. I found no conflicts with the transcript.

question: How did JPMorgan's full-year 2026 NII ex-Markets guidance change between the 1Q26 and 2Q26 calls, and why?
expected: ~$95B (held on 1Q) raised to ~$96.5B on 2Q, driven mainly by deposit balances rather than rates.

result.answer:
JPMorgan raised full-year 2026 NII ex-Markets guidance by $1.5 billion, from about $95 billion to about $96.5 billion.

**1Q26 call:** Management said it continued to expect NII ex-Markets of about $95 billion. Total NII was cut to about $103 billion because Markets NII fell to about $8 billion, mainly on rates. [1]

**2Q26 call:** Management said it now expected NII ex-Markets of about $96.5 billion. Total NII rose to about $105.5 billion, with Markets NII up to about $9 billion. [2]

**Why it rose (Barnum, Q&A):**
- The biggest single factor was deposit balances across Wholesale and Consumer. This covers both the overall amount and a mix shift toward slightly higher-margin deposits. [3]
- Rates were also a little higher than when JPMorgan last guided, at both the short end and the back end. [3]
- Actual rate sensitivity is probably a bit more than the earnings-at-risk (EaR) measure suggests, because consumer betas are outperforming the model. He said that gap is probably concentrated in the front end. [3]
- He summarized it this way: "a little bit of the increase as a function of higher rates, but most of it is balances overall." [4]
- The new guidance implies a higher exit run rate. That assumes the yield curve follows the forwards and deposit and other drivers match current expectations. [3]

**Analyst notes:** Joe Smith's and Sally Barton's 2Q26 notes both report the $96.5 billion figure and attribute it mostly to deposit balances. [5][6] That matches the transcript. Joe Smith's note also gives the prior figure as $95 billion. [5]

Sally Barton's 2Q26 note says Card NCO guidance rose to about 3.6%. That is outside your question, but it conflicts with the transcript, which says about 3.2% on better-than-expected credit performance. [2]

citations.passage: In terms of the full year 2026 outlook, we continue to expect NII ex. Markets to be about $95 billion. We now expect total NII to be approximately $103 billion, as a function of Markets NII decreasing to about $8 billion, predominantly due to rates, which we expect will be primarily offset in NIR.

In terms of the full year 2026 outlook, we now expect NII ex. Markets to be about $96.5 billion and total NII to be approximately $105.5 billion as a function of Markets NII increasing to about $9 billion.

Just mechanically in terms of the drivers of the upward revision, the biggest single factor is deposit balances, I would say, across both Wholesale and Consumer, both sort of the overall quantum of it, but also like mix shift inside of that in favor of slightly higher margin overall.
So, when you assemble that together, you have a little bit of the increase as a function of higher rates, but most of it is balances overall.

question: How did Azure growth in FY27 Q1 compare with what Microsoft guided on the FY26 Q4 call?
expected: Guided ~45% cc; delivered 48%, ahead of expectations despite 3P capacity delays.

result.answer:
Azure grew 48% in FY27 Q1, about 3 points above the roughly 45% Microsoft guided on the FY26 Q4 call.

- Guidance (FY26 Q4 call): Amy Hood said Microsoft expected "revenue growth of approximately 45% in constant currency" for Azure [1]. That followed 43% growth in FY26 Q4 [2].
- Actual (FY27 Q1 call): Hood said Azure revenue "was ahead of expectations and increased 48%, even with the 3P capacity delays" [3].
- Drivers of the beat: Foundry revenue more than tripled year-over-year. GPU-fleet efficiency gains let Microsoft allocate additional capacity to customers. Higher revenue per token and better CPU monetization also helped [3].
- Basis of comparison: the 48% is stated without a constant-currency label in the excerpt I found, while the 45% guide was in constant currency. Hood said FX was "roughly in line with guidance," so the gap is probably small [4].
- Analyst notes: Joe Smith and Sally Barton both report Azure at 48% and describe it as an acceleration. Neither contradicts the transcript [5][6].

Looking ahead, Microsoft guided Azure to 49–50% in constant currency for FY27 Q2 [7].

citations.passage: In Azure, we expect revenue growth of approximately 45% in constant currency and we remain focused on delivering efficiencies that help us bridge the gaps we see as customer demand continues to exceed supply.

Azure revenue was ahead of expectations and increased 48%, even with the 3P capacity delays noted earlier, driven by Foundry and improved CPU monetization.
And FX was roughly in line with guidance.

question: Did JPMorgan raise its full-year 2026 expense guidance on the 1Q26 call?
expected: No - held at ~$105B (Joe Smith's note wrongly says raised to ~$107B). It was raised to ~$107.5B on the 2Q26 call.

result.answer:
No. On the 1Q26 call JPMorgan held its full-year 2026 adjusted expense outlook at about $105 billion. CFO Jeremy Barnum said it "continues to be about $105 billion" [1]. He said the strong Markets and Banking results might otherwise have led the firm to revise the expense guidance up. He added that not revising it was "just a little early in the year" and that the firm would see how things play out over the next quarter or so [2][3]. The raise came on the 2Q26 call, when the outlook went up by $2.5 billion to about $107.5 billion. Barnum attributed the increase mainly to higher volume- and revenue-related expenses [4].

Analyst note discrepancy: Joe Smith's 1Q26 note says management "raised the full-year adjusted expense guide to about $107B" on that call. That is wrong, because the transcript shows the guide stayed at about $105B [5]. Sally Barton's 1Q26 note correctly says the ~$105B guide was kept [6].

And the new adjusted expense outlook is about $107.5 billion, with the increase primarily due to higher volume- and revenue-related expenses, driven by the activity levels and associated revenue outperformance.

question: How fast is Netflix's advertising business growing in 2026?
expected: Over 80% this year (behind internal target); Sally Barton's note says >100%, which conflicts.

result.answer:
Netflix says its ads business is growing over 80% in 2026. On the 3Q26 call, Greg Peters said, "We're still growing, our ads business over 80% this year." [1] That is below the company's own plan. He said Netflix is "currently a bit behind our aggressive target for the year." [1]

Analyst notes on the 3Q26 call:
- Joe Smith's note says ads are "still growing over 80% this year" but trail the company's target because partner integrations and new ad products are delayed. This matches the transcript. [2]
- Sally Barton's note says Peters said the business is growing "over 100% this year." That is wrong. The transcript says over 80%. [3]

The transcript gives no ad revenue dollar figure and no quarterly ad growth rates. Management also said ads are one of three revenue levers (members, pricing and ads) behind full-year 2026 revenue growth of 13–14%. [4]
